FOREIGN LLC/CORPORATION QUALIFICATION TO TRANSACT BUSINESS IN CALIFORNIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Holdings, LLC

FOREIGN QUALIFICATION INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Holdings, LLC, a limited liability company originally formed under the law of Delaware, with a principal office at 100 Market Street, Suite 400, Wilmington, DE. It describes California's statutory requirement that an out-of-state ("foreign") corporation or limited liability company register with the California Secretary of State before transacting intrastate business in California, along with the meaning of that phrase and the consequences California law attaches to transacting business here without first registering. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, or Statement of Information document. Those documents concern an entity being formed under California law in the first place, or an already-California-qualified entity's periodic reporting to the Secretary of State after formation or qualification. This document instead concerns an entity formed under the law of another state or jurisdiction that is separately registering to transact business in California without becoming a California entity. California maintains two distinct statutory frameworks for this registration, one in the General Corporation Law for foreign corporations and one in the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act for foreign limited liability companies; this document addresses both. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself register Acme Holdings, LLC, or any other entity, with the California Secretary of State, and it does not determine whether Acme Holdings, LLC's specific activities in California do or do not constitute "transacting intrastate business" within the meaning of California law.

REQUIREMENT FOR A FOREIGN CORPORATION TO OBTAIN A CERTIFICATE OF QUALIFICATION
California's General Corporation Law states that a foreign corporation shall not transact intrastate business in California without first having obtained a certificate of qualification from the Secretary of State. That certificate is obtained by filing a statement and designation by foreign corporation, on a form the Secretary of State prescribes, signed by a corporate officer or, for a foreign association that has no officers, by a trustee. This filing requirement applies to a corporation formed under the law of another U.S. state, another country, or any jurisdiction other than California, once that corporation is transacting intrastate business in California, a term California law defines separately.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A foreign corporation shall not transact intrastate business without having first obtained from the Secretary of State a certificate of qualification. To obtain that certificate it shall file, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement and designation signed by a corporate officer or, in the case of a foreign association that has no officers, signed by a trustee stating:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a), California General Corporation Law, Chapter 21 (Foreign Corporations), certificate-of-qualification requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2105.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's foreign-corporation qualification requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific corporation's obligations; other states impose their own, differently worded foreign-qualification requirements. This clause quotes a single subsection, Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a), so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a certificate of qualification or file the statement and designation described here on behalf of any entity, and it does not determine whether any specific corporation's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business."

REQUIRED CONTENT OF A FOREIGN CORPORATION'S STATEMENT AND DESIGNATION
The statement and designation a foreign corporation files to obtain its certificate of qualification must state: the corporation's name (and, if that name does not comply with California's naming rules, an alternate name adopted for use in California); the state or place of its incorporation and a statement that it is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges there; the street address of its principal office; the street address of its principal office in California, if it has one; its mailing address, if different from those addresses; and the name of an agent in California upon whom process directed to the corporation may be served. California also requires the statement and designation to include the corporation's irrevocable consent to service of process on that designated agent, and on the Secretary of State if the agent cannot be found, and a disclosure if the corporation will be subject to the Insurance Code as an insurer. Separately, the corporation must annex to the statement and designation a certificate from an authorized public official of its state or place of incorporation confirming that it is an existing corporation in good standing there.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(1) The name of the corporation, and, if the name does not comply with Section 201, an alternate name adopted pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2106. (2) The state or place of its incorporation or organization and a statement that the foreign corporation is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges in that state or place of its incorporation or organization. (3) The street address of its principal office. (4) The street address of its principal office in California, if any. (5) The mailing address of its principal office, if different from the addresses specified pursuant to paragraphs (3) and (4). (6) The name of an agent upon whom process directed to the corporation may be served within this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a), California General Corporation Law, content required in a foreign corporation's statement and designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2105.)
  "(b) Annexed to the statement and designation shall be a certificate by an authorized public official of the state or place of incorporation of the corporation to the effect that the corporation is an existing corporation in good standing in that state or place or, in the case of an association, an officers’ certificate stating that it is a validly organized and existing business association under the laws of a specified foreign jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(b), California General Corporation Law, annexed certificate of good standing requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2105.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's foreign-corporation application requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific corporation's obligations; other states impose their own, differently worded application requirements. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2105(a) for the content of the statement and designation itself and § 2105(b) for the annexed certificate of good standing, and treats them as one source, not as two independent corroborating sources. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself prepare, sign, or file the statement and designation described here on behalf of any entity, and it does not determine whether any specific corporation's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business."

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "TRANSACTING INTRASTATE BUSINESS"
California defines "transacting intrastate business" separately for foreign corporations and for foreign limited liability companies, in near-identical terms. For a foreign corporation, and only for purposes of the chapter of the General Corporation Law governing foreign corporations, "transact intrastate business" means entering into repeated and successive transactions of the corporation's business in California, other than interstate or foreign commerce. For a foreign limited liability company, and only within the meaning of the article of the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act governing foreign limited liability companies, a company that enters into repeated and successive transactions of business in California, other than in interstate or foreign commerce, is considered to be transacting intrastate business. Under both definitions, a single or isolated transaction, and business conducted across state lines rather than within California, are treated differently from a repeated, ongoing pattern of business conducted within the state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) For the purposes of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100), “transact intrastate business” means entering into repeated and successive transactions of its business in this state, other than interstate or foreign commerce."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 191(a), California General Corporation Law, statutory definition of "transact intrastate business" for foreign corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=191.)
  "(a) A foreign limited liability company that enters into repeated and successive transactions of business in this state, other than in interstate or foreign commerce, is considered to be transacting intrastate business in this state within the meaning of this article."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, parallel definition for foreign limited liability companies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.03.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines this term for its own foreign-qualification statutes — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific entity's activities, and not a claim that other states, or other California statutes, use this identical definition. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Corp. Code § 191(a) defines the term for foreign corporations, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(a) defines it, in separately worded but substantively similar terms, for foreign limited liability companies. These are treated as two independent, entity-type-specific sources, not as one source standing in for the other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's activities in California constitute "transacting intrastate business" under either definition.

ACTIVITIES THAT DO NOT CONSTITUTE TRANSACTING INTRASTATE BUSINESS
California's statutes list specific activities that, without excluding other activities that might also fall outside the definition, do not by themselves make a foreign corporation or foreign limited liability company one that is "transacting intrastate business" in California. For a foreign corporation, that list covers: maintaining or defending any action, suit, or administrative or arbitration proceeding, or settling claims or disputes; holding board or shareholder meetings or otherwise carrying on activities concerning its internal affairs; maintaining bank accounts; maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of its own securities; effecting sales through independent contractors; soliciting or procuring orders that require acceptance outside California before becoming binding contracts; creating evidences of debt or liens or security interests on property; and conducting a single, isolated transaction completed within 180 days that is not part of a number of repeated transactions of a similar nature. The parallel list for a foreign limited liability company is substantively similar and adds two further items not listed for corporations: securing or collecting debts or enforcing security interests in property securing those debts, and transacting business in interstate commerce. Separately, both statutes state that merely holding a status — being a shareholder of a corporation, a limited partner of a limited partnership, or a member or manager of a limited liability company that itself transacts intrastate business — does not, by itself, make the shareholder, partner, member, or manager a transactor of intrastate business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(c) Without excluding other activities that may not constitute transacting intrastate business, a foreign corporation shall not be considered to be transacting intrastate business within the meaning of subdivision (a) solely by reason of carrying on in this state any one or more of the following activities: (1) Maintaining or defending any action or suit or any administrative or arbitration proceeding, or effecting the settlement thereof or the settlement of claims or disputes. (2) Holding meetings of its board or shareholders or carrying on other activities concerning its internal affairs. (3) Maintaining bank accounts. (4) Maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of its securities or depositaries with relation to its securities. (5) Effecting sales through independent contractors. (6) Soliciting or procuring orders, whether by mail or through employees or agents or otherwise, where those orders require acceptance outside this state before becoming binding contracts. (7) Creating evidences of debt or mortgages, liens or security interests on real or personal property. (8) Conducting an isolated transaction completed within a period of 180 days and not in the course of a number of repeated transactions of like nature."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 191(c), California General Corporation Law, activities that do not constitute transacting intrastate business for foreign corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=191.)
  "(b) Without excluding other activities that may not be considered to be transacting intrastate business in this state within the meaning of this article, activities of a foreign limited liability company that do not constitute transacting intrastate business in this state include all of the following: (1) Maintaining or defending any action or suit or any administrative or arbitration proceeding, or effecting the settlement of those, or the settlement of claims or disputes. (2) Carrying on any activity concerning its internal affairs, including holding meetings of its members or managers. (3) Maintaining accounts in financial institutions. (4) Maintaining offices or agencies for the transfer, exchange, and registration of the limited liability company’s own securities or maintaining trustees or depositories with respect to those securities. (5) Selling through independent contractors. (6) Soliciting or procuring orders, whether by mail or electronic means or through employees or agents or otherwise, if the orders require acceptance outside this state before they become contracts. (7) Creating or acquiring indebtedness, evidences of indebtedness, mortgages, liens, or security interests in real or personal property. (8) Securing or collecting debts or enforcing mortgages or other security interests in property securing the debts and holding, protecting, or maintaining property so acquired. (9) Conducting an isolated transaction that is completed within 180 days and is not in the course of a number of repeated transactions of a like nature. (10) Transacting business in interstate commerce."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, parallel activities list for foreign limited liability companies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.03.)

This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Corp. Code § 191(c) lists the carve-out activities for foreign corporations, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.03(b) lists the separately worded, substantially parallel carve-out activities for foreign limited liability companies; they are treated as two independent, entity-type-specific sources. Each statute also states expressly that its list does not exclude other activities that may likewise fall outside the definition, so an activity's absence from this list does not mean it constitutes transacting intrastate business. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's specific activities in California fall within or outside this carve-out list.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF A FOREIGN LLC'S APPLICATION FOR CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION
A foreign limited liability company registers to transact business in California by delivering an application for a certificate of registration to the Secretary of State, on a form the Secretary of State prescribes. The application must state: the company's name (and, if that name does not comply with California's naming rules, an alternate name adopted for use in California); the state or other jurisdiction under whose law the company is organized and a statement that it is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges there; and the street address of the company's principal office, and of its principal office in California, if it has one. California's Limited Liability Company Act does not, at this section, contain a single sentence stating outright that a foreign LLC "shall not" transact intrastate business without registering, the way the corporation statute does; instead, the obligation to register functions through the application requirements described here together with the litigation-related and injunctive consequences described elsewhere in this document. Separately, the company must deliver with its application a certificate of existence, status, or good standing (or a record of similar import), issued within the past six months, from the official who has custody of its public records in its home jurisdiction. California law also makes clear that receiving a certificate of registration does not authorize a foreign limited liability company to engage in any business, or exercise any power, that a California limited liability company itself could not engage in or exercise here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A foreign limited liability company may apply for a certificate of registration to transact business in this state by delivering an application to the Secretary of State for filing on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State. The application shall state all of the following: (1) The name of the foreign limited liability company, and, if the name does not comply with Section 17701.08, an alternate name adopted pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 17708.05. (2) The state or other jurisdiction under whose law the foreign limited liability company is organized and a statement that the foreign limited liability company is authorized to exercise its powers and privileges in that state or other jurisdiction. (3) The street address of the foreign limited liability company’s principal office and of its principal office in California, if any."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, content required in a foreign LLC's application for a certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.02.)
  "(b) A foreign limited liability company shall deliver with a completed application under subdivision (a) a certificate of existence, status, or good standing or a record of similar import, issued within the past six months from the submission of the application for filing in California, signed by the Secretary of State or other official having custody of the foreign limited liability company’s publicly filed records in the state or other jurisdiction under whose law the foreign limited liability company is formed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(b), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, certificate of existence or good standing requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.02.)
  "(c) A certificate of registration does not authorize a foreign limited liability company to engage in any business or exercise any power that a limited liability company shall not engage in or exercise in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.01(c), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, scope of authority conferred by a certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.01.)

CONSEQUENCES FOR A FOREIGN CORPORATION TRANSACTING BUSINESS WITHOUT QUALIFYING
California law attaches several distinct consequences to a foreign corporation transacting intrastate business without holding a valid certificate of qualification. First, the corporation may be subject to a civil penalty of $20 for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted, and by transacting that unauthorized business, the corporation is deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of California's courts in any civil action arising in California in which it is named a defendant. Second, and separately, a corporation that transacts intrastate business without complying with the certificate-of-qualification requirement is barred from maintaining any action or proceeding, in a California court, upon the intrastate business it transacted — but only for an action or proceeding commenced before it complies. That bar lifts once the corporation has complied with the qualification requirement, paid a $250 penalty to the Secretary of State (in addition to the filing fees otherwise due), and filed with the court receipts showing payment of that penalty, those fees, and any franchise or other taxes on business or property that should have been paid for the period it transacted business unqualified. The statute barring the corporation from maintaining an action does not, by its terms, prevent other parties from suing the unqualified corporation, and does not state that the underlying business the corporation transacted is void or unenforceable — only that the corporation itself cannot affirmatively maintain an action on it until it complies. Third, transacting intrastate business without complying with the qualification requirement is separately a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $500 and not more than $1,000, prosecuted by the Attorney General or a district attorney.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Any foreign corporation which transacts intrastate business and which does not hold a valid certificate from the Secretary of State may be subject to a penalty of twenty dollars ($20) for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted; and the foreign corporation, by transacting unauthorized intrastate business, shall be deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of the courts of California in any civil action arising in this state in which the corporation is named a party defendant."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2203(a), California General Corporation Law, per-day monetary penalty and deemed consent to California court jurisdiction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2203.)
  "(c) A foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) which transacts intrastate business without complying with Section 2105 shall not maintain any action or proceeding upon any intrastate business so transacted in any court of this state, commenced prior to compliance with Section 2105, until it has complied with the provisions thereof and has paid to the Secretary of State a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) in addition to the fees due for filing the statement and designation required by Section 2105 and has filed with the clerk of the court in which the action is pending receipts showing the payment of the fees and penalty and all franchise taxes and any other taxes on business or property in this state that should have been paid for the period during which it transacted intrastate business."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2203(c), California General Corporation Law, bar on maintaining an action until compliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2203.)
  "Any foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 which transacts intrastate business without complying therewith is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by fine of not less than five hundred dollars ($500) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), to be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 2258, California General Corporation Law, misdemeanor criminal penalty for transacting business without complying with Chapter 21 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=2258.)

CONSEQUENCES FOR A FOREIGN LLC TRANSACTING BUSINESS WITHOUT REGISTERING
California's Limited Liability Company Act attaches its own set of consequences to a foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business without a certificate of registration, and those consequences are not identical to the corporation statute's. A foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business in California may not maintain an action or proceeding in California unless it holds a certificate of registration — but lacking a certificate does not prevent the company from defending an action or proceeding brought against it. The statute also states expressly that a member or manager of the company is not personally liable for the company's debts, obligations, or other liabilities solely because the company transacted intrastate business without a certificate of registration. And if the company transacts intrastate business without a certificate, or cancels a certificate it previously held, it is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of that intrastate business. Unlike the corporation statute, this article does not itself set out a specific per-day or fixed-dollar civil penalty, or a separate misdemeanor criminal penalty, for a foreign limited liability company that transacts intrastate business without registering. It does, however, give the Attorney General a separate enforcement tool: the Attorney General may bring an action to enjoin a foreign limited liability company from transacting intrastate business in California in violation of the Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business in this state shall not maintain an action or proceeding in this state unless it has a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business in this state. (b) The failure of a foreign limited liability company to have a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business in this state does not prevent the foreign limited liability company from defending an action or proceeding in this state. (c) A member or manager of a foreign limited liability company is not liable for the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the foreign limited liability company solely because the foreign limited liability company transacted intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration. (d) If a foreign limited liability company transacts intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration or cancels its certificate of registration, it shall be deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of the transaction of intrastate business in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.07(a)-(d), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, consequences of transacting intrastate business without a certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.07.)
  "The Attorney General may maintain an action to enjoin a foreign limited liability company from transacting intrastate business in this state in violation of this title."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.09, California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Attorney General's authority to enjoin unauthorized intrastate business (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17708.09.)

This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.07(a) through (d), and treats them as one source, not as four independent corroborating sources; it separately cites Cal. Corp. The observation that this article does not itself set out a per-day or fixed-dollar civil penalty, or a criminal penalty, parallel to the corporation statute's is a statement about the absence of such a provision in the specific sections reviewed for this document, not a survey of every provision anywhere in California law that could conceivably apply to an unregistered foreign LLC's conduct. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific limited liability company has transacted intrastate business without a certificate of registration, or what consequence, if any, would apply to any specific company's conduct.

expectedJSON.body: California law attaches several distinct consequences to a foreign corporation transacting intrastate business without holding a valid certificate of qualification. First, the corporation may be subject to a civil penalty of $20 for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted, and by transacting that unauthorized business, the corporation is deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of California's courts in any civil action arising in California in which it is named a defendant. Second, and separately, a corporation that transacts intrastate business without complying with the certificate-of-qualification requirement is barred from maintaining any action or proceeding, in a California court, upon the intrastate business it transacted — but only for an action or proceeding commenced before it complies. That bar lifts once the corporation has complied with the qualification requirement, paid a $250 penalty to the Secretary of State (in addition to the filing fees otherwise due), and filed with the court receipts showing payment of that penalty, those fees, and any franchise or other taxes on business or property that should have been paid for the period it transacted business unqualified. The statute barring the corporation from maintaining an action does not, by its terms, prevent other parties from suing the unqualified corporation, and does not state that the underlying business the corporation transacted is void or unenforceable — only that the corporation itself cannot affirmatively maintain an action on it until it complies. Third, transacting intrastate business without complying with the qualification requirement is separately a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than $500 and not more than $1,000, prosecuted by the Attorney General or a district attorney.

citations.quote: (a) Any foreign corporation which transacts intrastate business and which does not hold a valid certificate from the Secretary of State may be subject to a penalty of twenty dollars ($20) for each day that unauthorized intrastate business is transacted; and the foreign corporation, by transacting unauthorized intrastate business, shall be deemed to consent to the jurisdiction of the courts of California in any civil action arising in this state in which the corporation is named a party defendant.

citations.quote: (c) A foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) which transacts intrastate business without complying with Section 2105 shall not maintain any action or proceeding upon any intrastate business so transacted in any court of this state, commenced prior to compliance with Section 2105, until it has complied with the provisions thereof and has paid to the Secretary of State a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) in addition to the fees due for filing the statement and designation required by Section 2105 and has filed with the clerk of the court in which the action is pending receipts showing the payment of the fees and penalty and all franchise taxes and any other taxes on business or property in this state that should have been paid for the period during which it transacted intrastate business.

citations.quote: Any foreign corporation subject to the provisions of Chapter 21 which transacts intrastate business without complying therewith is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by fine of not less than five hundred dollars ($500) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), to be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction.

expectedJSON.body: California's Limited Liability Company Act attaches its own set of consequences to a foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business without a certificate of registration, and those consequences are not identical to the corporation statute's. A foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business in California may not maintain an action or proceeding in California unless it holds a certificate of registration — but lacking a certificate does not prevent the company from defending an action or proceeding brought against it. The statute also states expressly that a member or manager of the company is not personally liable for the company's debts, obligations, or other liabilities solely because the company transacted intrastate business without a certificate of registration. And if the company transacts intrastate business without a certificate, or cancels a certificate it previously held, it is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of that intrastate business. Unlike the corporation statute, this article does not itself set out a specific per-day or fixed-dollar civil penalty, or a separate misdemeanor criminal penalty, for a foreign limited liability company that transacts intrastate business without registering. It does, however, give the Attorney General a separate enforcement tool: the Attorney General may bring an action to enjoin a foreign limited liability company from transacting intrastate business in California in violation of the Act.

(b) The failure of a foreign limited liability company to have a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business in this state does not prevent the foreign limited liability company from defending an action or proceeding in this state. (c) A member or manager of a foreign limited liability company is not liable for the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the foreign limited liability company solely because the foreign limited liability company transacted intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration. (d) If a foreign limited liability company transacts intrastate business in this state without a certificate of registration or cancels its certificate of registration, it shall be deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for rights of action arising out of the transaction of intrastate business in this state.
